articles.title: Democratic rep tells ABC, CBS to 'grow a spine' after Kimmel announces alternative Talarico interview
articles.summary: California Rep. Ted Lieu accused ABC and CBS of "bending the knee" after Jimmy Kimmel shifted his James Talarico interview off-air in a pair of deleted X posts.
articles.body: Rep. Ted Lieu, D-Calif., attacked ABC, CBS and other networks in a pair of deleted X posts Thursday after hearing reports about Jimmy Kimmel's upcoming interview with Democratic Texas U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico. The late-night host announced Wednesday night he would be interviewing Talarico. But, out of concern for the FCC under President Donald Trump, he added that he would be releasing the interview on YouTube instead of airing it on his show, "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" Lieu accused ABC and other networks, like CBS, of "bending the knee" to authoritarians by refusing to air interviews of elected officials. JIMMY KIMMEL RETURNS FROM LENGTHY HIATUS WITH DEFIANT MESSAGE TO FCC CHAIR BRENDAN CARR "Dear @ABC, @CBS and other networks: Grow a f---ing spine. Air whatever interviews with elected officials you want. You will win in court. Bending the knee to an authoritarian Administration only makes things worse. I assume you will now never air an interview of Trump as well?" Lieu wrote. "You know what else you can do @ABC and @CBS? Offer Ken Paxton the opportunity to come onto late night talk shows where the hosts can legitimately skewer Paxton by asking him about all his scandals. But instead you groveled and chose the path of self-censorship. Shameful." Fox News Digital reached out to ABC, CBS and Lieu's office for comment but did not immediately receive responses. Kimmel similarly accused the FCC of targeting his show and ABC based on "guest bookings it would seem they don’t like." DISNEY SUES FCC OVER ‘RETALIATORY CAMPAIGN AGAINST ABC,’ SEEKS TO BLOCK EARLY RENEWAL PROCEEDINGS "Now that he’s president, his FCC has threatened me, threatened our show, threatened our network, ABC, our affiliates, our local stations, based on traditional simple editorial decisions, guest bookings it would seem they don’t like," Kimmel said. "And, so, out of consideration for our local stations, especially our ABC affiliates in Texas who have to deal with this nonsense, my interview tomorrow with James Talarico will not air on television. It will be posted on YouTube instead. It will not be on TV." The situation was reminiscent of former late-night host Stephen Colbert's interview with Talarico ahead of the Texas Senate primary, in which Talarico competed against Texas Rep. Jasmine Crockett. Colbert's show, which has since been canceled, did not air the interview with Talarico and only posted it to the show's YouTube channel in February. Colbert announced at the time that CBS had stopped the show from airing the interview. However, FCC Chairman Brendan Carr clarified to Fox News at the time that the interview would have potentially violated the equal-time rule, which requires broadcast stations to provide equal opportunities to opposing political candidates during an election season. COLBERT LASHES OUT AT CBS, SAYS CANCELLATION ‘REINFORCED A NARRATIVE’ OF ‘KNEE BENDING’ TO TRUMP In a comment to Fox News Digital, Curtis Houck, managing editor at NewsBusters, suggested Kimmel could land in "hot water" for his stunt to move around the equal-time rule and avoid speaking with Talarico's GOP opponent, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. "Jimmy Kimmel thinks he's being cute or even brave by thumbing his nose at the FCC, but he's likely to end up in hot water for this. The equal time rules are what they are," Houck said. "Kimmel and his clapping seals in the liberal, elitist media are telling on themselves when they try to explain away the record of Kimmel and his fellow network late-night hosts as virulent partisans with guest disparities that can only be rivaled by ABC's ‘The View.’" CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital also reached out to the FCC and Talarico and Paxton's respective campaigns for comment.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy's lawyer torches conspiracy theories accusing Patrick Clancy
articles.summary: Lindsay Clancy's attorney defended Patrick Clancy, rejecting conspiracy theories and arguing evidence cited by prosecutors does not prove the killings were premeditated.
articles.body: Lindsay Clancy's defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, forcefully defended Patrick Clancy in a new interview with Fox News, rejecting online speculation that the father of three was somehow involved in the deaths of his children, calling the ordeal he endured "horrific." Speaking to Fox News' Bryan Llenas after the mistrial in Lindsay Clancy's murder case, Reddington said he has continued to hear claims accusing Patrick Clancy despite years of investigation. "My response to those people is, at some point, maybe you get a chance to listen to that 911 tape, and then you look me in the eye and tell me that you think Patrick Clancy did this," Reddington said. "What this guy has been through is horrific." When asked if there was "no way" that Patrick Clancy was responsible, Reddington doubled down. LINDSAY CLANCY'S LAWYER REVEALS POST-MISTRIAL STRATEGY AS RETRIAL LOOMS "I've never said he did. I never would say he did. I don't think the evidence shows that he did," Reddington responded. "I know what the evidence shows as far as postpartum. That's the defense in this case." Reddington also rejected suggestions that Patrick Clancy was neglectful or failed to support his wife before the deaths of the couple's three children. "How was he neglectful?" Reddington said. "The man was with her, took her to the doctors, tried to advocate on her behalf, was supportive of her." He said Patrick Clancy witnessed Lindsay Clancy struggle with sleeplessness and other symptoms that the defense has argued were consistent with severe postpartum mental illness. Reddington also defended Patrick Clancy's decision to remarry after the horrific deaths of his children, saying he's "entitled to move on with his life." It is something that Lindsay Clancy herself understands. LINDSAY CLANCY JUROR WHO BACKED THE DEFENSE ALSO PUBLICLY CHEERED KAREN READ'S ACQUITTAL "She has no compunction whatsoever about saying anything bad about Patrick Clancy," he said of his client. The case has garnered widespread attention, especially online, where intense debate and speculation have fueled conspiracy theories about what happened. Reddington also pushed back on one of the prosecution's central arguments that Lindsay Clancy carefully planned the killings by sending Patrick Clancy out on errands. The defense attorney argued that theory was inconsistent with the evidence, pointing to Apple Maps searches prosecutors highlighted during the trial. "The government takes the position that this was planned," Reddington said. "Well then, why would she Google the distance of nine minutes and three minutes to CVS?" DAYS AFTER LINDSAY CLANCY MISTRIAL ANOTHER MASSACHUSETTS MOM ACCUSED OF KILLING HER CHILDREN SEEKS FREEDOM Reddington argued that if Lindsay Clancy had intended to kill the children, she would not have needed to wait for Patrick Clancy to leave the house. "This woman, if she wanted to plan this, she could have killed those children while he was downstairs working," he said. "It's ridiculous." LINDSAY CLANCY LAWYER SAYS HE PLANS NEW MOTION TO DISMISS AFTER JURORS SPEAK OUT ON MISTRIAL: REPORT Reddington also offered an alternative explanation for the Apple Maps searches, saying Lindsay Clancy was overwhelmed after spending the day caring for her children and wanted to know when her husband would return home. "She was spinning out of control and needed him home," Reddington said. "It was bath time. It was the time to put the kids to bed. She had to know that he was coming back." He said the searches were consistent with the defense's argument that Lindsay Clancy was struggling with severe postpartum mental illness rather than carrying out a calculated plan. "If she was, she would have Googled as she did, and she would've been spot on on every single symptom of postpartum psychosis," Reddington said. "She was telling the truth." Reddington also dismissed claims that Lindsay Clancy fabricated hearing a voice to bolster her postpartum psychosis defense. Critics had argued the reported voice seemed convenient, a theory Reddington rejected. LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE "You have a very intelligent woman who we all know was Googling all over the place about psychosis," Reddington said. "She was Googling about the medications. She was Googling about the side effects. SEND US A TIP "I know some people want to see her electrocuted. They want to see her thrown into a pond and tied to a log like they used to do to the witches and see if they float. … These people can crawl back into their basements and say what they want. I don't care." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The comments came days after a Massachusetts jury deadlocked in Lindsay Clancy's murder trial, resulting in a mistrial. Prosecutors have said they intend to retry the case, while the defense is pursuing motions seeking dismissal of the charges or a reduction in the murder counts before any retrial proceeds.

articles.title: Practical Magic 2 star: 'People long for simpler times'
articles.summary: Actresses Maisie Williams and Joey King feature in the upcoming sequel of the 1998 fantasy romcom.
articles.body:
Mix together a beloved film simmering for decades, a sprinkling of social media hype and a generous glug of star power and you just might conjure up the long-awaited sequel to Practical Magic.

The 1998 fantasy romcom, starring Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman as witchy sisters Sally and Gillian Owens, received mixed reviews from critics when it was first released.

But it's put a spell on a new generation discovering it online, with some now regarding the film as a cult classic and autumn staple.

The demand for a follow-up by this new wave of fans helped convince Bullock and Kidman to reprise their roles nearly 30 years on, they say.

"You never get the opportunity to do something where people really are asking you, 'please do it'," says Bullock. "It's usually us going to them."

Actresses Joey King and Maisie Williams are joining the cast this time round to play Sally's daughters, Kylie and Antonia.

Kissing Booth star King tells BBC Newsbeat she feels this desire for nostalgic content, which has become one of the defining forces within entertainment in recent years, has been influenced by "the world moving so fast".

"I think with technology moving at the speed that it is, we're really missing the times when we were less reachable," she says.

"If we couldn't figure out something, we'd stare out the window until it came to us, and I think we're nostalgic for a time like that."

She feels this can also be a strength of cinema as it can help "make memories" and "feelings" for people that they can revisit by rewatching.

The upcoming release comes at a time when reboots, reunions and remakes are dominating film and TV lists.

Game of Thrones star Williams agrees the drive for nostalgic content feels like a "symptom of people longing for simpler times", but says she is "very grateful" that they have made a sequel and not a remake.

"I do believe in pushing the story forwards and I do believe in telling new stories," she says.

"And I do believe stories can come back around and they can still be meaningful.

"But I am not the biggest fan of the remake because I think it's a shame to withhold ourselves from telling a new story."

Practical Magic 2 sees the cast return to a world which is steeped in powerful ancestral magic with the characters once again confronting a family curse which condemns anyone who loves and is loved by an Owens woman to death.

There are also nods to the original throughout, with bubbling family tension, dark romantic "witchcore" fashion and the iconic midnight margaritas.

US acting stalwarts Dianne Wiest and Stockard Channing return to their roles for the follow-up, while Guardians of the Galaxy actor Lee Pace, Cobra Kai's Xolo Maridueña and House of the Dragon's Solly McLeod are new additions.

Reviews so far have been mixed, with the Guardian describing it as a "nostalgia-bait return" which is as "strange and messy as the first" but with "warm seasonal pleasures to be had".

Meanwhile The Hollywood Reporter says the "slapdash" sequel "works better the less you look for any sense of logic, and the more you just lean into the transient joys of watching these actresses bounce off each other".

Amid the scrutiny around the film, Williams admits joining the Practical Magic world was "a little bit overwhelming", but says the cast were "so supportive the whole time" and "welcomed us into the sisterhood".

The bond of sisterhood is at the heart of the first film and continues in the sequel, but Bullock has recalled this was initially one of the criticisms of the original , with some branding it as "too witchy" with "too many women".

With women's rights under pressure in some countries, Williams says it is a "challenging time" and she feels it's "so important in a time like this for women to be supporting one another".

"We are in a time when young women are staying in education longer and women, before having children, are sometimes being paid more than their male counterparts, which I do find to be really exciting," she adds.

"And this feeling of witches, symbiosis and power - I feel like there's something in that which can just push us forwards."

articles.title: Why is Uber pulling out of some African markets?
articles.summary: Uber’s exits from Nigeria and Uganda highlight the growing challenges of making ride-hailing work in Africa.
articles.body:
Abuja, Nigeria – Uber is leaving Nigeria and Uganda just as the cost of running a ride-hailing business is becoming harder to sustain in parts of Africa.

The company ended its 12-year run in Nigeria and about a decade in Uganda on September 2 , saying the decision followed a “thorough review” of its business priorities and was limited to those countries. Reuters reported that Uber did not provide specific reasons for the Nigeria exit.

But the latest pullouts follow a series of exits from African markets. After six years in Ivory Coast, Uber left last year and ended its Tanzania service in January this year after nearly a decade there.

The closures do not point to a simple lack of demand. Instead, they highlight a harder calculation: whether platforms can keep fares affordable for passengers, whether drivers can earn enough to stay on the road and whether commissions are high enough to make the business worthwhile?

Why did Nigeria become so difficult for Uber drivers?

President Bola Tinubu’s economic reforms, including the removal of the fuel subsidy and changes to the naira’s exchange-rate regime, have reshaped the cost of doing business in Nigeria.

For ride-hailing drivers, petrol, imported spare parts and vehicle maintenance have become more expensive, squeezing incomes at a time when fares remain under pressure.

The frustration came to a head in March, when drivers working for Uber, rivals Bolt and inDrive staged a three-day strike in Lagos and Ogun over what they described as unsustainable fares and poor working conditions.

Uber driver Farouk Adebayo, who joined the strike in Lagos, told Al Jazeera how the economics had changed.

“Since the government removed the subsidy, I have really been struggling with making a profit with Uber the way I used to. When I add the cost of maintaining my car and everything else, the profit I was making from driving with Uber was not worth it.”

For drivers, the problem was not simply what Uber charged. It was the accumulation of costs on top of the platform’s commission.

Ayoade Ibrahim, co-founder and general secretary of the Amalgamated Union of App-Based Transporters of Nigeria (AUATON), said drivers were being squeezed from several directions.

“Talk to any driver and you hear the same arithmetic. The platform takes 25–30 percent commission. Then fuel. Then maintenance. Then insurance. Then the occasional fine. What remains is barely enough to feed a family, let alone save for the next repair. That is why so many drivers told us, as a union, that they had already migrated to Bolt and inDrive, or gone offline to negotiate cash trips simply to survive,” Ibrahim said.

That shift matters because Uber is competing not only for passengers, but also for drivers who can move between platforms.

Bolt and inDrive are major competitors in Nigeria, alongside local platforms, such as Rida and LagRide.

inDrive allows passengers and drivers to negotiate fares, while its global model has generally involved a service fee of about 10 percent.

For drivers, the ability to switch platforms, or leave them altogether, gives them an alternative when commissions or fares become unattractive.

That makes the market harder for platforms to navigate as operating costs rise. A large customer base can generate plenty of rides without necessarily generating enough margin.

Uganda presents a different market but a familiar problem.

The Smart Online Drivers Association resisted platform commissions in 2019 when it petitioned parliament over what it described as exploitative practices. Drivers were particularly concerned about Uber’s 25 percent commission while fares remained low.

Bolt and SafeBoda were already established competitors in Kampala before Uber’s departure. Smaller platforms, including Faras, Yango and Tinka, have increased the competition.

Uber entered the Ugandan market in 2016 and later launched UberBODA.

The challenge, as in Nigeria, is not necessarily finding passengers. It is keeping the three sides of the business, passengers, drivers and the platform satisfied enough for the model to remain viable.

Uber has not said that Nigeria or Uganda were unprofitable, nor has it provided a detailed country-by-country explanation for the exits.

Instead, it says it is focusing investment on markets where it can provide earning opportunities for drivers at scale and where riders can travel seamlessly. The company stressed that it remains committed to sub-Saharan Africa.

Kenya shows why pulling out is not inevitable.

In 2022, the Kenyan government introduced regulations to cap the commission of ride-hailing platforms at 18 percent. Uber had been charging 25 percent and after driver protests, the company cut its commission to 18 percent.

Rather than leave, the company changed the economics of its operation.

That suggests Uber’s calculation varies from market to market. Where it sees enough long-term value, it can respond to pressure by changing fares, commissions or other parts of its model. Where the economics no longer justify that investment, leaving becomes an option.

Nigeria has a huge population – 237 million – and substantial demand for urban transport. Uganda has a growing urban market. Tanzania and Ivory Coast had their own opportunities.

For ride-hailing platforms, the calculation is ultimately simple: passengers want affordable journeys, drivers need enough income to cover their costs and the company needs a commission large enough to sustain its service.

When that balance breaks down, drivers look elsewhere, passengers follow cheaper options and the platform loses leverage.

Uber’s exits from Nigeria and Uganda, following the leaving of Tanzania and Ivory Coast, point to a more selective approach to Africa.

For now, Uber says it remains committed to the continent. But its future may increasingly depend not on how much demand it can find, but on which markets can make the economics work.

For Ibrahim, the calculation ultimately comes back to the people behind the wheel.

“Uber’s model was built on independent contractors bearing almost all cash costs. In markets with stable fuel prices and accessible vehicle finance, that can work. In Nigeria, where the cost of a full tank can swing tens of thousands of naira in a month, it does not. Drivers become the shock absorbers for the macroeconomy.”

articles.title: Family of critically missing DC mother says police still treating home as active crime scene
articles.summary: Antoinette Forbes' sister says alarming discoveries inside the Washington, D.C., home prompted police to reclassify her as critically missing.
articles.body: The sister of a Washington, D.C., mother who vanished last week said a series of alarming discoveries inside her home immediately signaled something was wrong as police continue investigating her disappearance after reclassifying her case as a critically missing person. Antoinette Forbes, 53, was last seen around 3 p.m. Friday at her home in the 3200 block of Nebraska Avenue NW, according to the Metropolitan Police Department. Police are asking anyone with information about her whereabouts to come forward. According to family friend Elizabeth Northrup, police initially classified Forbes as a missing person before reclassifying her as critically missing in less than 24 hours. Under Metropolitan Police Department guidelines, a critically missing person is someone believed to be in danger or facing life-threatening circumstances. "I knew immediately something was wrong," Forbes' sister, Aileen Forbes, told Fox News Digital. 'WONDERFUL' CA NURSE AND MOTHER VANISHES AFTER GOING TO CASINO, CAR FOUND ABANDONED AT MOUNTAIN PARK: FAMILY The sisters had spoken over FaceTime on Saturday morning while making plans to visit their mother in Florida over the holidays. "It was just a fairly ordinary check-in with my sister, with whom I have regular contact — daily contact by text or on FaceTime," Aileen said. "We were just talking about our plans for the holidays." By Labor Day, Aileen said she had tested positive for COVID-19 and texted her sister because she has an underlying health condition that can make the illness more dangerous. When repeated texts and FaceTime calls went unanswered, she grew concerned. She contacted close family friends who live near Antoinette's Washington home. The friends, who had a key to the house, entered the home and immediately noticed several troubling signs. FAMILY CHECKS LAS VEGAS MORGUES IN DESPERATE SEARCH FOR MISSING NEW YORK GRANDMOTHER "The text I got from Margarita ... I think something happened to me that made my heart stop," Aileen said. The friends found Antoinette's dog, Max, alone inside the home after he had gone to the bathroom indoors, suggesting he had been left alone for some time, Aileen said. Her car remained in the driveway, while her phones and wallet were still inside the house. The family immediately contacted police. Aileen said investigators have told the family the home is being treated as an active crime scene and that no one, including relatives, has been allowed inside. NEW DETAILS REVEAL MARRIAGE IN CRISIS BEFORE ANA WALSHE MURDER CASE IN FOX NATION SPECIAL "No one has access to Antoinette's home, not even me," Aileen said. "In some ways, it's my home too, and I have not been able to step foot in it." She said detectives have not provided significant updates but have remained in contact with the family and continue accepting information that could aid the investigation. "I know that they have been working tirelessly since Monday afternoon ... around the clock," Aileen said. Aileen said nothing about her sister's life suggested she would voluntarily disappear. "Antoinette has a full, rich life," she said. "She's an incredibly successful woman professionally, personally. She's a happy woman." She described her sister as a devoted mother whose world revolved around her 10-year-old son, Nathan, and the family's dog, Max. Asked what she would say if her sister could hear her, Aileen responded, "Antoinette, you know how much we love you. You know who loves you. Keep the faith. We are not going to give up. We are going to bring you home." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Police describe Forbes as 5 feet, 2 inches tall, weighing approximately 115 pounds, with black hair and brown eyes. Anyone with information about her whereabouts is urged to contact the Metropolitan Police Department.

articles.title: Maduro’s wife seeks home detention as heart condition worsens in US custody
articles.summary: Her lawyers say Flores needs cardiac treatment and recovery facilities a detention centre cannot provide.
articles.body:
Venezuela’s former first lady, Cilia Flores de Maduro, has asked a judge to release her from federal detention in the United States, citing a worsening heart condition.

In an application for pre-trial release on Wednesday, her legal team asked for the court to allow Flores to await trial under home confinement in Manhattan.

It described her declining health since US military operation on January 3 that resulted in her abduction from Caracas and imprisonment in New York, as well as that of her husband, former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro.

“Prior to the United States’ military invasion of Venezuela, Ms. Flores de Maduro was physically healthy and took no ongoing medication, other than a monthly injection to help control her mitral valve prolapse,” the legal filing said.

“Now she is prescribed four medications, maintains nitroglycerin by her side in the event of a potential heart attack, and grapples with the continued medical advice suggesting coronary exploration and surgery.”

Flores was a prominent figure in her husband’s government, serving as first lady since his inauguration in 2013.

Prior to Maduro’s first inauguration, she was also a leading member of the United Socialist Party of Venezuela (PSUV), the country’s dominant political movement, leading the National Assembly for more than four years.

But Maduro had long clashed with the administration of US President Donald Trump, who accused Venezuela of sending drug-traffickers into the US. Both Maduro and Flores have also faced allegations of participating in human rights abuses, including the violent suppression of political dissent.

After launching a one-day military operation to abduct Maduro and Flores, the Trump administration charged them both with drug- and weapons-related charges. They are currently awaiting trial in New York City.

But Flores’s health has been in doubt since her forced removal from Venezuela, according to her legal team.

After consulting outside medical experts, Flores’s lawyers said they believe she may have suffered a minor heart attack on July 29 while in US custody.

They also questioned whether she was receiving the appropriate medical care for her mitral valve prolapse, a condition affecting one of the heart’s valves.

Since her imprisonment, her lawyers said Flores has not received the monthly injection she needs to manage the condition.

Instead, she has reportedly been prescribed baby aspirin, a statin, diltiazem and nitroglycerin to use when she experiences chest pain.

Doctors have recommended that she undergo a cardiac procedure, which could result in additional heart operations. If she undergoes such treatment, Flores “will need adequate time to recover from any procedures in a setting conducive to restoring her health”, her lawyers said.

Thursday’s filing acknowledges that Flores does not “dispute that she has received excellent care” from medical professionals. But it argues that “a detention centre lacks the conditions needed for such a recovery”.

Her lawyers proposed moving Flores from the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn to a residence within the Manhattan federal court district, where she and Maduro are due to go on trial next June.

Under home detention, Flores would be subject to round-the-clock armed monitoring, with visits restricted to people approved by the court and federal prosecutors. Her home would also be monitored by video and her phone calls recorded, according to the filing.

Judge Alvin K Hellerstein has yet to rule on the application.

Flores, 69, and Maduro, 63, have been held in US custody since the January raid on their home in Caracas. Both have pleaded not guilty to the charges of participating in a conspiracy to traffic cocaine into the US.

articles.title: Knoxville nonprofit leaders take on 120-mile hike in Spain, raising money for 'Homes of Love'
articles.summary: Dr. Gary Chesney and his wife, Debbie, are co-founders of Homes of Love, a Knoxville nonprofit that supports family-structured homes for orphaned and at-risk...
articles.body:
Dr. Gary Chesney and his wife Debbie, co-founders of Homes of Love, are hiking the Camino de Santiago in Spain to raise money for their nonprofit supporting orphaned and at-risk children in Vietnam, Cambodia, and Zimbabwe.

The couple's inspiration for their mission came from Debbie's high school experience of seeing the impact of the Vietnam War on orphaned children, leading them to adopt their sixth child from Vietnam and start Homes of Love to provide children with loving families.

The Chesneys have raised enough funds from their hike to bring five children into their program, with a goal of $25,000 to help 10 children find safety, love, and compassion in family-structured homes.

One Knoxville dentist traded his dental chair for hiking boots — walking more than 100 miles across Spain to raise money and awareness for a nonprofit he and his wife started 25 years ago.

Dr. Gary Chesney and his wife, Debbie, are co-founders of Homes of Love , a Knoxville nonprofit that supports family-structured homes for orphaned and at-risk children in Vietnam, Cambodia and Zimbabwe.

The couple's mission has deep personal roots.

Debbie says her heart for children in Vietnam began when she was in high school and saw the impact of the Vietnam War on children who were left behind.

"I was in high school and it was a black and white TV on WBIR, and I saw just the plight of orphans that had been left from the war," she said. "That deeply impacted me."

"She was in an orphanage with like 300 other children, and she was actually well taken care of, but we would never want her to grow up in an orphanage," Debbie said.

That experience helped inspire Homes of Love, which now works to place children who are unwanted, neglected, abused or without someone to care for them into loving families.

"They're not orphans anymore. They belong. They have a place. They're safe. They're growing up in a family," Debbie said.

Now, Dr. Gary Chesney is putting one foot in front of the other for that mission.

He and Debbie have been hiking the Camino de Santiago in Spain, covering 120 miles over eight days, with one day left and 10 miles to go.

Gary says the hike is especially meaningful after dealing with knee problems for decades.

"I feel like God touched my life, or touched my knees," Gary said. "This is the first time I've ever enjoyed walking."

The couple set a $25,000 fundraising goal, which would help them bring 10 children into Homes of Love. Gary says all money raised from this trip goes directly towards the nonprofit.

So far, they say they've raised enough to bring five children into the program.

"Just to see the difference in these children that have found safety, love and compassion from parents. I've received so many blessings from just being able to watch," Debbie said. "They're not orphans anymore. They belong. They have a place. They're safe."

You can donate directly to Homes of Love here .

articles.title: Restaurant chain once frequented by Kardashians files for bankruptcy after 36 years
articles.summary: A 36-year-old Southern California brunch chain filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, owing over $1 million after rent disputes and construction woes forced multiple closures.
articles.body: Another longtime American restaurant chain is fighting to keep its doors open as mounting debt and financial losses batter the dining industry. Marmalade Cafe, a 36-year-old Southern California brunch favorite, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection Sept. 2, citing "rent disputes and mounting supplier debts." It owes more than $1 million to Gilmore Farmers Market, US Foods, Sysco Ventura Inc., the California Department of Tax and Fee Administration and others, according to multiple reports. The Encino-based company listed total assets of $12.7 million in the filing but reported a net loss of $680,314, according to the New York Post. LONGEST-RUNNING RED LOBSTER LOCATION IN AMERICA IS CLOSING AFTER 56 YEARS Over the years, the chain, which first opened in Santa Monica in 1990, evolved from a grab-and-go spot to offering private dining and catering to businesses, including Boeing, Mattel, CBS and Warner Bros. Studios. The Calabasas location was even a favorite of the Kardashians, according to reports. It was operating just four locations across Southern California at the time of the filing after closing four others in recent years. The company cited hardships, including "unsustainable financial losses and a lack of rent relief," according to the filing. BEFORE MCDONALD'S AND STARBUCKS, AMERICANS PACKED THESE ONCE-BELOVED LUNCH COUNTERS The Calabasas restaurant closed after construction disrupted parking and drove down sales; its Santa Monica location shuttered amid losses tied to the Palisades Fire; and the Original Farmers Market outpost closed after failing to regain pre-pandemic business, the Los Angeles Times reported. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "Unfortunately, the ongoing construction throughout the shopping center has resulted in a devastating decline in business," the restaurant wrote in a Facebook post in July about the Calabasas closure. "Despite our best efforts to weather these challenges, and after seeking rent relief from our landlord during this extended construction period, the landlord declined to help," the statement continued. "With construction expected to continue for an extended period, we simply cannot sustain the financial losses any longer." That closure was reportedly a main catalyst for the bankruptcy filing. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Marmalade Cafe's four remaining locations in El Segundo, Malibu, Sherman Oaks and Westlake Village remain open, and a representative told the Los Angeles Times they are "very healthy and very strong." Longtime restaurants are being squeezed by simultaneous increases in rent, wages, insurance and utilities, chef Andrew Gruel, founder of American Gravy and a Huntington Beach city councilman, told Fox News Digital. "Marmalade's Chapter 11 filing is a prime example of how difficult the restaurant business has become, particularly in California," Gruel said. "Longevity and a loyal customer base are valuable, but they don't necessarily protect a restaurant when the underlying cost structure changes faster than the business can adapt." The filing also stated that the company had downsized from more than 200 employees to about 50 as of this year. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Marmalade Cafe is the latest in a string of restaurant bankruptcies and closures across the Golden State and nationwide. Other recent casualties include Fireman Hospitality; Salad and Go; FAT Brands, the parent company of Fatburger; Johnny Rockets and other chains. Red Lobster, Carl's Jr. and On the Border locations have also recently shuttered. The closures do not necessarily mean the restaurants were poorly run, Gruel added. Rather, rising costs can catch up with even established businesses, part of an industry reset he expects will bring more closures. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "The operators who survive will likely be those who can adapt their menus, staffing, hours, footprint and overall business model while maintaining the experience that brings customers back," he said. Fox News Digital reached out to Marmalade Cafe for comment.

articles.title: Juror on Lindsay Clancy trial says 'we let down Lindsay' following mistrial
articles.summary: A Lindsay Clancy trial juror says the jury "let down Lindsay" after a lone holdout prevented a unanimous not guilty verdict in Massachusetts.
articles.body: A juror on the high-profile Lindsay Clancy murder trial in Massachusetts said she believes the jury "let down Lindsay" and that it was "hard to separate the children from what our task was." Clancy was on trial for strangling and killing her three young children in January 2023 after sending her then-husband, Patrick, out to pick up medication and takeout. When he returned, he found Clancy injured outside after an apparent suicide attempt and the children unconscious in the basement. Two children died that night, while the third was airlifted to a Boston hospital and died several days later. The trial ended in a mistrial last week after the jury failed to reach a unanimous verdict. Eleven jurors sided with finding Clancy not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility — Massachusetts’ version of an insanity defense — while one holdout favored finding her criminally responsible. "Everybody says you're not supposed to feel like you failed, but you have a task to come out unanimous. And we tried everything we could to get to that end. And I feel like we let down Lindsay," Paula, 65, who was one of the jurors who sided with the majority, told WCVB. LINDSAY CLANCY LAWYER SAYS HE PLANS NEW MOTION TO DISMISS AFTER JURORS SPEAK OUT ON MISTRIAL: REPORT Clancy's legal team did not dispute that she killed her children but argued that she should not be found criminally responsible because she was suffering from postpartum psychosis. Clancy also admitted in court filings to killing her three children, but claimed that severe mental illness left her not criminally responsible. Paula said the jury's majority believed that Clancy needed help and that the healthcare system failed her, adding that she thinks the medical community should do more to support women with postpartum mental health issues. "There was a clear indication that the medical community failed her and not just her, but her whole family, because something like that affects the whole entire family. And if everybody can be educated in a better way, then it will help the whole family unit," Paula said. After attorneys made their arguments, Paula said the jurors were sent to deliberate with 297 pieces of evidence, including Patrick's emotional 911 call, which she said some jurors had trouble listening to during deliberations. "We all tried to help each other. It was hard to separate the children from what our task was, and it was very emotional," she said. The jurors polled themselves at the start of deliberations, at which point eight believed Clancy was not guilty due to lack of criminal responsibility, two thought she was guilty and two were undecided, Paula said. The majority eventually came to the belief that Clancy was not guilty due to lack of criminal responsibility. Prosecutors argued during trial that Clancy was criminally responsible for the killings despite evidence that she suffered from mental illness. "We did not start out 11 to one," Paula said. "Everybody had different opinions and different reasons and different ways that they got there." Paula said the majority had a hard time understanding why the one holdout wanted to vote to convict Clancy. "We did not feel that he was following the law because he admitted that he had doubt at different times, that he had doubt about the case that was presented, and the way that the rule read to all the rest of us is if we had doubt, then we could not convict her of first-degree murder or second-degree murder or manslaughter," Paula said. The foreperson then sent a note to the judge saying the jury could not reach a verdict and accusing the holdout of refusing to apply the law on reasonable doubt. Judge William Sullivan called up each of the jurors and individually asked them if they could apply the law as he had explained it, and they reportedly answered in the affirmative. "The judge has to believe that people are telling him the truth. And so, you know, 11 people told the truth and one maybe didn't. And I will never know why," Paula said. Paula said she believed it would have been worth restarting deliberations with an alternate if the court had removed the holdout. ACCUSED NC KILLER MOM PLANS INSANITY DEFENSE — AS RETIRED JUDGE SAYS MORE MAY FOLLOW LINDSAY CLANCY STRATEGY "If our holdout juror had given us evidence to support his reasoning, we would have felt differently about what we told the judge," Paula said. Other jurors have also spoken out in recent days to take issue with the holdout's position. "He had the hardest time getting off the fact that Lindsay viciously killed her children," juror Kellie Farina previously told NBC10 Boston. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP On Thursday, Clancy's defense filed a motion arguing the prosecution failed to meet its burden and asked the judge to enter a required finding of not guilty, which the defense argues would prevent a retrial.

articles.title: Fire in eastern Congo kills at least 26 students at 2 schools
articles.summary: BUKAVU, Congo — A fire swept through two adjacent schools Thursday in the city of Bukavu in eastern Congo, killing at least 26 students and injuring dozens, the provincial government said.
articles.body: BUKAVU, Congo — A fire swept through two adjacent schools Thursday in the city of Bukavu in eastern Congo, killing at least 26 students and injuring dozens, the provincial government said. The South Kivu provincial government said in a press release that 19 girls and seven boys were killed, adding that the death toll could rise. The spokesperson for rebel M23 group that controls the city, Lawrence Kanyuka, said earlier that 24 students were killed and 29 people were being treated at local medical facilities. The fire started at a house before spreading to the two adjoining schools, local neighborhood administrator Moïse Lubala told The Associated Press. He said several students were trapped inside Furaha secondary school and some suffocated. A mix of boys and girls of different ages, students at Furaha and at Ujamaa primary school, were brought to the Nyamulagira BDOM health center in their school uniforms, nurse Ciza Jean-Baptiste told the AP. Medical staff were struggling to keep track of the exact number of injured because there were so many, he said. “The exit was too narrow, so some students began jumping through windows while others rushed toward the door. As everyone tried to force their way out, students were pushed over and trampled on,” said Lubala. The cause of the fire is not known, but the neighborhood where the fire started is densely populated and most houses are made out of wood, according to Lubala. Congo’s government struggles to exert control over the east of the country. M23 rebels, backed by Rwanda, took control of Bukavu in February 2025. More than 100 armed groups are vying for control of eastern Congo’s trillions of dollars in mineral wealth that’s critical for much of the world’s technology. Health services are under severe strain as the region grapples with the deadliest Ebola outbreak in history that has killed more than 3,300 people, with more than 6,800 confirmed cases recorded.

articles.title: MPs to vote on legalising assisted dying in England and Wales
articles.summary: The proposal was backed by a majority of MPs earlier this year but did not become law after its progress was stalled by peers.
articles.body:
The legalisation of assisted dying in England and Wales could move a step closer on Friday when MPs vote on a proposal to introduce it.

The bill would allow adults with fewer than six months to live to apply to be given help to end their own life, subject to certain safeguards.

Labour MP Lauren Edwards, the bill's sponsor, said there was a "real human cost to the delay" in passing the legislation - but opponents say it lacks sufficient safeguards, particularly for vulnerable people.

The last effort to change the law was supported by MPs but stalled in the House of Lords earlier this year after peers tabled more than 1,200 amendments.

Edwards said she was asking MPs to send the same law "back to the House of Lords so that they can finish what they started".

She said the Lords has an "important role in scrutinising, refining and often improving legislation" sent to them by the Commons, adding: "Let them amend this bill if they choose to and send it back to MPs for a final decision.

"That is how our democratic decisions are made and what should happen now.

"There is a real human cost to the delay in passing this legislation and correcting the injustices and cruelty of the current law."

Veteran broadcaster Dame Esther Rantzen, a high-profile campaigner for assisted dying, called on MPs to support the bill, saying her own life with terminal cancer had become "unbearable" .

The 86-year-old said she was too frail to travel to an assisted suicide clinic in Switzerland as she had planned to, saying: "Everything I didn't want to happen I'm having to go through now."

Why are MPs voting on assisted dying again?

Safeguards within the bill include a requirement that a person applying for an assisted death has the approval of two doctors and an expert panel.

But critics say it includes too few measures to protect vulnerable people from being coerced into ending their lives, while some improving palliative care should be the priority.

Labour MP Ashley Dalton said she did not support the bill first time around and it "remains deeply flawed and unsafe".

She added: "I have very serious concerns about people, especially vulnerable people, being pressured or coerced into assisted dying. The safeguards within this bill are not enough to support them."

The leader of Catholics in England and Wales, Archbishop Richard Moth, called the proposal "wrong in principle" and "deeply flawed". The Church of England's Archbishop of Canterbury, Dame Sarah Mullally, wrote in the Telegraph that it would signal "we are a society that believes that some lives are not worth living".

Some medical organisations, including the Royal College of Psychiatrists and the Royal College of Physicians, have also said they have "concerns" about the bill's built-in guardrails.

Marie Curie, Hospice UK and St Christopher's hospice charity have all said they are neutral on the principle of assisted dying, but have repeatedly warned that access to quality of end-of-life care is too patchy across the country and the sector is severely lacking in funding.

Friday's second reading debate will allow MPs to consider the main principles of the bill and they must start voting before 14:30 BST.

If they vote in favour it will have cleared its first major hurdle and the next stage will allow MPs to consider possible amendments at committee stage.

However, their support could be conditional - just because an MP votes in favour of the bill at this stage in the proceedings, it does not mean they will do so at the third reading.

If MPs vote against the bill on Friday, it will fall. Supporters of assisted dying have said they would make another attempt to pass legislation as soon as was possible.

Both sides expect the result to be close and it could depend on how many MPs turn up for the sitting on Friday, a day when they would usually expect to be in their constituencies.

During the last parliamentary session, the bill was brought forward by Labour MP Kim Leadbeater and cleared the House of Commons on 20 June 2025 with a majority of 23.

Support for the bill fell between the second and third readings, before it stalled in the House of Lords.

Backers of the bill accused some peers of using delaying tactics to block the proposal, while critics argued it was not fit for purpose due to a lack of safeguards.

Opponents believe support for the bill in the Commons has weakened since the last attempt to pass it failed.

Edwards said she wanted to bring forward a bill that was identical to the one approved by the Commons last year. Under the terms of the Parliament Acts, if an identical bill passes the Commons in two successive parliamentary sessions then the Lords cannot halt its progress a second time.

Peers can still suggest amendments which, if agreed by the Commons, would be added to the bill.

Labour MPs Gareth Snell, who backed the bill last time, and Dame Meg Hillier, a prominent opponent of assisted dying, have co-signed a letter to colleagues voicing their concerns over the risks of the possible use of the Parliament Acts.

They warned MPs were "potentially being presented with a 'this or nothing' ultimatum on Friday".

Edwards has argued she does not want to use the Parliament Acts but MPs passing an identical bill would force peers to scrutinise the legislation without being able to halt its progress.

Opponents have warned that using this procedure would risk creating a law which disability charities, hospices and others have raised major concerns over.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will not vote on the bill on Friday , describing it as "a matter for Parliament to decide" and stressing that the government would officially remain neutral.

He has previously said he personally believes that funding for end-of-life care in the UK should be improved before legalising assisted dying is considered.

articles.title: Singer D4vd sued by parents of teen girl he is accused of killing
articles.summary: Celeste Rivas Hernandez’s parents are suing the singer D4vd, accusing him of wrongful death after he was charged in the 14-year-old girl’s murder.
articles.body: Celeste Rivas Hernandez’s parents are suing the singer D4vd, accusing him of wrongful death after he was charged in the 14-year-old girl’s murder. Mercedes Martinez and Jesus Rivas are also suing D4vd’s mother and managers, accusing them of negligence. D4vd’s real name is David Anthony Burke. The lawsuit, filed Thursday in Los Angeles County Superior Court, outlines much of the evidence presented at a multiday evidentiary hearing in July about the pair’s relationship, which prosecutors said began when Celeste was 13 and ended after she threatened to expose him. Text messages revealed at the hearing showed that she had gotten pregnant by Burke and had an abortion. Her decomposed and dismembered remains were found in September 2025 in the front trunk of Burke’s Tesla at a Los Angeles impound lot. Prosecutors said the car had been left on a street near his home and impounded at Hollywood Tow after someone reported an abandoned vehicle. Burke, 21, was arrested in April at a house in the Hollywood Hills neighborhood, Los Angeles police said. He has pleaded not guilty to charges of murder, continuous sexual abuse of a child under the age of 14 and unlawful mutilation of human remains. He remains in custody awaiting trial. The lawsuit accuses Burke of using his position of authority to “influence and control” Celeste, “including by providing her a concealed cellular telephone to maintain contact outside her parents’ knowledge, using false identities, and arranging and paying for her travel.” The suit says that on the night she died in April 2025, Burke sent an Uber vehicle to pick her up from her family’s home in Lake Elsinore in Riverside County. After she arrived at his home in the Hollywood Hills, Burke stabbed her, prosecutors allege. Prosecutors said he used chain saws to cut her body apart in his garage. Celeste’s parents say in the lawsuit that because of the decomposition, they had to wait more than a week after her remains were found for an identification and that some parts of the body were never recovered. The suit accuses Burke of wrongful death, as well as battery, sexual battery, childhood sexual assault, assault, false imprisonment, human trafficking and intentional infliction of emotional distress. It also alleges that Burke engaged in human trafficking by causing or inducing Celeste “to engage in commercial sex acts.” “The money, food, shelter, designer gifts, travel, a ring, and a promise of future marriage that Burke gave to Decedent were given on account of the sexual acts, satisfying the commercial-sex-act element,” the suit says. “Because Decedent was a minor, neither her purported consent nor any mistakes as to her age is a defense.” Burke’s publishing and merchandising companies are also named as defendants in the lawsuit, which claims they were the vehicles that helped fund the alleged abuse. Listed as co-defendants are Josh Marshall and Robert Morgenroth, Burke’s managers; their company, Mogul Vision; and Burke’s live-in security guard, who the suit alleges drove him to pick up Celeste from her parents’ home in 2024. The suit also lists Burke’s mother, Colleen Burke, as a co-defendant and says she approved and funded “arrangements that housed Decedent and enabled Burke’s access to her.” All co-defendants are accused of failing to protect a minor and negligence. It was not immediately clear whether Burke had an attorney representing him in the lawsuit. Contact information could not be found for Burke’s companies or his security guard. Marshall, the owner of Mogul Vision, which employed Morgenroth, did not immediately respond to a request for comment on behalf of himself, the company or Morgenroth. Messages left at numbers believed to be associated with Morgenroth and Colleen Burke were not immediately returned. The suit requests a jury trial. Celeste’s parents asked for the death penalty this week. “If the death penalty were activated, it would be perfect for this kind of human being, devoid of feelings ... and without conscience, who only caused pain to our daughter, our family, and the world that supports our precious daughter,” they said in a statement on what would have been Celeste’s 16th birthday.

articles.title: Charlie Kirk supporters return to site of assassination 1 year later: ‘We are still standing’
articles.summary: Turning Point USA returned to Utah Valley University to reclaim the space where Charlie Kirk was assassinated, unveiling a new statue in his honor.
articles.body: One year after Charlie Kirk was assassinated at Utah Valley University, the people who stood feet from him when he was killed returned to the campus Thursday night in what Turning Point USA (TPUSA) described as a deliberate effort to "reclaim" the space in his honor. "We’re doing an event in Utah right now at UVU, a deliberate act reclaiming that space in his honor and for his legacy," TPUSA spokesman and "The Charlie Kirk Show" Executive Producer Andrew Kolvet told Fox News host Jesse Watters Thursday night. Andrew Sypher, TPUSA’s chief field officer, told the gathering at UVU in Orem that he had been standing about 10 feet to Kirk’s left when the fatal shot rang out on Sept. 10, 2025. CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSINATION: NEW UVU PRESIDENT SAYS IT WILL CONTINUE TO ‘HOST THE FRAYS,’ EMBRACE FREE SPEECH "Steps from these doors is the ground where evil unfolded," Sypher said. "We did not come back to rehearse the crime scene." Instead, Sypher said, they returned because "this is where they tried to end him" and "this is where we refuse to let the last word be a gunshot." ERIKA KIRK URGES CONSERVATIVE STUDENTS NOT TO BACK DOWN IN FIRST SCHOOL YEAR SINCE CHARLIE'S ASSASSINATION For the students of UVU’s TPUSA chapter, the anniversary marked a return to the campus where some witnessed Kirk’s assassination. "A year ago, our lives changed forever," chapter President Sage Lloyd told the crowd. Lloyd said students experienced "fear, grief, confusion, and heartbreak" and had every reason to walk away. INSIDE CHARLIE KIRK’S EFFORT TO DEVELOP THE NEXT GENERATION OF CONSERVATIVE VOICES "We could have packed our bags. We could have stepped away," she said. Despite the tragedy, the TPUSA chapter stayed. "The same students who witnessed a political assassination are willing to stand up, speak out and keep moving forward," Lloyd said. "We can let it define us through fear, or we can let it strengthen us through courage," she added. "The Turning Point chapter at UVU has made our decision, and we chose courage." Sypher also revealed what he said was a text Kirk sent him on the morning he was assassinated. SURVEILLANCE VIDEO TIMELINE TRACKS ACCUSED CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSIN ACROSS UVU CAMPUS BEFORE FATAL ROOFTOP SHOT "Andrew, I’m not here to pick a fight. I am here to show them kindness," Kirk wrote, according to Sypher. "That was the assignment this time," Sypher said. "To talk with students who hate you. To share the truth, and to not become cruel doing it." Soon afterward, Kirk was fatally shot. "Charlie’s assassination did not put our faith to death," Sypher told the crowd. "It woke it up." The service was marked with worship performances and video tributes to the fallen conservative leader, as well as an unveiling of a new statue to stay on campus at UVU. ERIKA KIRK PENS ESSAY ON GRIEF AS READERS GAIN INSIGHTS INTO WRENCHING PAST YEAR Kirk’s widow, Erika Kirk, separately marked the anniversary with a black-and-white photograph from their wedding showing the couple holding hands. Across the image were two words: "...until Heaven." The university closed its campus for the one-year anniversary. UVU itself did not organize the memorial, but university President Dr. Jon Anderson previously told Fox News Digital the school supported TPUSA using campus space for its event. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Lloyd closed her remarks with a message about what returning to UVU meant for Kirk’s student movement. "Our chapter is still here, we are still speaking, and we are nowhere near done," she said. "And that is how his voice lives on." Fox News Digital's Michael Ruiz contributed to this reporting.

articles.title: Organizers of Hong Kong’s Tiananmen vigils sentenced to up to 7 years and 3 months in national security case
articles.summary: Three pro-democracy activists in Hong Kong who organized annual vigils for victims of China’s 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown were sentenced Friday under a national security law that critics say has stifled dissent.
articles.body: HONG KONG — Three pro-democracy activists in Hong Kong who organized annual vigils for victims of China’s 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown were sentenced to prison terms between five and over seven years Friday after being convicted under a national security law that critics say has stifled dissent in the Chinese territory. Lee Cheuk-yan was sentenced to seven years in prison, while Chow Hang-tung was sentenced to seven years and three months. Both had pleaded not guilty to charges of inciting subversion under the Beijing-imposed law. A third defendant, Albert Ho, 74, was sentenced to five years and two months after pleading guilty, which can result in a shorter sentence. Both Lee and Chow, who have been in custody continuously since they were charged five years ago, had pleaded for reduced sentences after the verdict. They had faced a maximum of 10 years in prison. All three were leaders of the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China, which for three decades held annual candlelight vigils in honor of those who were killed on June 4, 1989, in a Chinese military crackdown on pro-democracy protesters in and around Beijing’s Tiananmen Square. The vigils, which drew tens of thousands of people a year, were the only large-scale public commemoration on Chinese soil of the Tiananmen crackdown, discussion of which is heavily censored in mainland China. The alliance itself, which was also convicted, was fined 1.5 million Hong Kong dollars ($190,000) as part of the sentencing. The trial, which began in January, was heard by three government-appointed judges who ruled last month that the alliance’s longtime call to “end one-party dictatorship” in China was an unlawful form of incitement to overthrow the country’s ruling Communist Party. The United States, along with many other Western governments and the United Nations, condemned the Aug. 21 verdict as a further sign of Hong Kong’s deteriorating freedom of expression. The Tiananmen vigils “sought only to remember the past and honor the lives lost in that assault,” Assistant Secretary of State Riley Barnes said in a post on X. During the trial, Lee, 69, a former lawmaker, told the court that the alliance was not calling to eliminate the Communist Party, but rather to allow the Chinese public to decide who governs them through free and fair elections. The judges said the defendants were not being tried over their political views. Chow, 41, a barrister who represented herself in court, said in her mitigation statement that the 206-page verdict “boils down to saying that pursuing democracy is a crime.” “Believing that dictatorship is wrong and democracy is right — if that isn’t a belief, then what is?” she said. Chow added that she had “no regrets” about her activism, saying she “would rather be a criminal than a person who betrays their conscience.” Hong Kong, a former British colony, returned to Chinese rule in 1997 with the promise that its civil liberties would be preserved for at least 50 years. But residents of the once-freewheeling city have seen their freedoms significantly eroded since Beijing imposed a controversial 2020 national security law, which has also been used to jail other pro-democracy activists such as former media tycoon Jimmy Lai. Legal concerns have led to the shutdown of dozens of civil society groups, including the alliance, which voted to disband in 2021. In 2024, Hong Kong’s pro-Beijing leadership passed their own toughened national security legislation, known as Article 23, which critics say has only further chilled expression. Hong Kong and central Chinese authorities say the laws were necessary to restore stability in the city after months of anti-government protests in 2019 that sometimes turned violent. They say the Tiananmen vigil organizers continued to engage in criminal acts after the 2020 law took effect and that freedom of speech should not be used as a “pretext” for unlawful activities. The alliance “had long been deliberately planting seeds of hatred” against the Communist government and “inciting people to subvert state power,” John Lee, Hong Kong’s top leader, said after the verdict. The vigil was first banned in 2020 before the national security law took effect, with Hong Kong authorities citing Covid-19 restrictions. In more recent years, the former vigil site has been occupied around June 4 by a carnival organized by pro-Beijing groups. Each year there is heavy police presence at the site around the anniversary, and some people have been detained after showing up with flowers or candles. The Tiananmen crackdown has also been erased from public view in Hong Kong in other ways, with local universities removing Tiananmen sculptures and other artwork that had stood on their campuses for years and officials forcibly closing the city’s June 4th Museum. The conviction of the Tiananmen vigil organizers “symbolizes the fall of the rule of law in Hong Kong,” said Eric Lai, a senior fellow with the Georgetown Center for Asian Law, citing the handpicked judges, the lack of a jury and the defendants’ extended time in custody. He said the alliance verdict and other national security convictions had created a “gray zone” not just for activists, but for everyday people in Hong Kong because “words and deeds that we thought were constitutionally acceptable and lawful in the past could be a crime now.” Other cases linked to the 2019 protests remain unresolved. Last week, prominent activist Joshua Wong, 29, who is already serving a prison term of four years and eight months in a separate case, pleaded guilty to conspiracy to collude with foreign forces to endanger national security in a second prosecution against him. As of March, 386 people had been arrested under the Beijing and Hong Kong national security laws, with 176 people and four ​companies convicted, Reuters reported, citing the local Security Bureau. Some were arrested over social media posts whose criticism of the government was alleged to be seditious. Last week, national security police said they had arrested two men and one woman accused of “shouting seditious slogans” as they marked the Aug. 31 anniversary of a 2019 incident at a metro station during which Hong Kong police were accused of beating protesters, which they denied. If the three arrested people are charged, they could face up to seven years in prison.

articles.title: Hong Kong’s Tiananmen vigil organizers handed lengthy prison terms
articles.summary: Three key organizers behind what used to be the only large-scale public commemoration for the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre on Chinese soil will spend years in prison for inciting subversion in Hong Kong after judges handed down their sentence on Friday.
articles.body: Three key organizers behind what used to be the only large-scale public commemoration for the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre on Chinese soil will spend years in prison for inciting subversion in Hong Kong after judges handed down their sentence on Friday. Their imprisonment is the latest chapter in Beijing’s yearslong national security crackdown in Hong Kong underscoring the risks that now exist in the once outspoken city in commemorating the victims of a bloody event Chinese officials have spent decades trying to erase. The trio were key figures from a group that organized an annual vigil in Hong Kong that marked the moments when the ruling Chinese Communist Party sent in tanks to violently quell peaceful, student-led democracy protests in Beijing’s Tiananmen Square. The yearly gathering - where crowds thousands strong would often chant “end one party rule” and other pro-democracy slogans - was a vivid symbol that starkly differentiated the financial hub from the rest of mainland China. On Friday, West Kowloon Court sentenced Chow Hang-tung, a prominent young human rights lawyer to seven years and three months in prison, and former opposition lawmaker Lee Cheuk-yan to seven years in prison. They were found guilty last month. A third activist, veteran pro-democracy lawmaker Albert Ho - who pleaded guilty for a lighter sentence, an increasingly common strategy for those facing national security charges - received a five years and two months prison term. The group that used to organize the vigil - the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China - was also fined HK$1.5 million ($191,300). Before Friday’s sentencing, Chow posted a statement on her Patreon page saying her guilty verdict declared that “pursuing democracy is a crime.” “If doing so makes me a criminal for life – if the law truly cannot accommodate our beliefs – then I would rather be a criminal than a person who betrays their conscience,” she wrote. In a summary, the trial judges wrote that the trio’s offenses took place during “a turbulent and unsettled social atmosphere” and that their group spread “subversive” messages through other activities and social media. “Although the present cases did not involve violence or threat of violence, nor had the defendants put forward any specific means of implementation or timetable to carry out ‘end one-party dictatorship,’ the court found that the offense was still of a serious nature,” the judges wrote. A city transformed Hong Kong’s position as a once-outspoken corner of China has been upended in recent years by a national security law Beijing imposed following huge and often violent democracy protests that convulsed the city in 2019. The erasure of the city’s annual candle-light Tiananmen vigil is one of the most visible examples of the ensuing crackdown, which critics, human rights groups and multiple Western nations – including the United States – say has quashed dissent and ended the city’s unique freedoms. Beijing and the Hong Kong government say the national security laws were needed to return the city to order and stability. “The HKSAR Government strongly condemns any biased remarks and smears against the HKSAR’s effort for safeguarding national security,” a government spokesperson said in response to a CNN inquiry when the trio were first convicted, using Hong Kong’s official title, adding rights and freedoms are protected under the national security law. Chinese troops cracked down on pro-democracy protesters around Beijing’s Tiananmen Square on June 4, 1989. No official death toll has ever been released, but estimates range from several hundred to thousands, with many more injured. The subject remains widely censored inside China. Following the events of 1989, mourners would converge on the same day every year in Hong Kong’s Causeway Bay district, to attend a vigil that filled multiple soccer pitches in the neighborhood’s Victoria Park with candlelight, calling for greater democracy for China. It was a tradition that continued after Hong Kong’s 1997 handover by Britain to China, alongside frequent street protests and a political system that allowed pro-democracy lawmakers to stand. That tradition came to an end with the imposition of a series of new national security offenses in 2020, with civil groups disbanded, some independent media outlets forced to shut down, and most activists jailed or living in exile. But prosecutors said, and judges agreed, that the campaigns by the vigil organizers - including calls for an end to “one-party dictatorship” - amounted to an incitement to subversion. Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee - a former security chief - welcomed the verdict. “Their conspiracy was abundantly clear, which must be brought to justice,” he said last month. But human rights groups and multiple foreign nations - including the United States - condemned their conviction. Retiree Simon Ng, who had attended the Tiananmen vigils for decades, said he came to court on Friday with with a heavy heart, because a peaceful act of speech had now been made illegal. “Hundreds of thousands of people had attended them in the past. This is an accusation against all of them,” he told CNN. Zhou Fengsuo, a former student leader at the Tiananmen Square protests who now has US citizenship, told CNN the verdict showed “how profoundly Hong Kong has changed.” “Authorities can extinguish the candles in Victoria Park, but they cannot extinguish the memory of June 4,” he added.

articles.title: Putin lands in India for BRICs summit, shadowed by Iran and Ukraine wars
articles.summary: Russian, Iranian leaders due to hold talks with India’s Modi at summit dominated by wars in Middle East and Ukraine.
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin arrived in the Indian capital on Friday ahead of an 11-member BRICS summit set to be dominated by wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, as well as economic challenges.

Putin and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian are due to hold talks with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, while Chinese President Xi Jinping is also expected to meet Modi on the sidelines of the two-day meeting.

Putin arrived at Palam Air Force Station in New Delhi, where he was greeted by India’s Minister of State for External Affairs Kirti Vardhan Singh, according to footage broadcast by Russia’s Ria Novosti news agency.

Posters of a beaming Modi lined streets across New Delhi to welcome leaders, with heavy deployments of security forces across the capital and widespread traffic restrictions in central districts. Delhi police have urged people to be patient and cooperative.

BRICS, which stands for the original members of the grouping – Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa – was created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions dominated by Western powers.

It has since expanded, and now includes Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates – three countries with sharply differing positions on the US-Israel war on Iran launched in February.

“The Gulf conflict is going to be the central fault line this time during the BRICS summit,” Harsh V Pant of India’s Observer Research Foundation told the AFP news agency.

“What was seen until last year as an achievement – the expansion of BRICS – today looks like a big constraint on BRICS,” Pant said.

It will be Pezeshkian’s first visit to India as Iranian president, and will put the Middle East conflict firmly on the agenda. The Iranian president’s visit marks the first in eight years for the role.

“The war in Iran will provide a stern test of the (expanded) group’s cohesion,” Shilan Shah of Capital Economics told AFP, noting the failure of the BRICS foreign ministers to agree on a joint statement when they met in New Delhi in May.

India maintains cordial relations with Iran and Israel, but is also careful to strike a delicate balance in its ties with Washington.

India has navigated the energy crisis caused by the war on Iran in part by turning to Russia, one of its most important strategic partners and its most controversial fuel supplier in recent years, as Moscow’s war against Ukraine drags on.

Putin last visited India in December 2025, but he also met Modi in Bishkek, the capital of Kyrgyzstan, this month.

Indian Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar visited Kyiv this month, where Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he was “grateful to India for its commitment to ending this unjust war”.

For China’s Xi, it will be his first visit to India since 2019, and marks the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between the rival neighbours, six years after a deadly military clash along their disputed Himalayan border.

Ties between the nuclear-armed Asian giants have been warming again recently, with flights, visas and high-level contacts gradually being restored.

However, deep mistrust remains, with their contested frontier, a widening trade deficit and strategic rivalry still complicating ties.

articles.title: How 'white-coat terror' module unfolded: Al-Falah doctors first tested bombs inside university, then in Aravalis
articles.summary: GURGAON: Test blasts on Al-Falah University campus, in open field, experiments deep inside the Aravalis, allegedly marked the progression of a “white-.
articles.body: GURGAON: Test blasts on Al-Falah University campus, in open field, experiments deep inside the Aravalis, allegedly marked the progression of a “white-coat” terror module linked to three Al-Falah University doctors, according to the NIA chargesheet in the Red Fort blast case.Dr Umer Un Nabi, Dr Muzammil Shakeel Ganaie and Dr Adeel Ahmed Rather allegedly tested explosive mixtures and firearms in isolated locations around Faridabad as they moved from experimenting with fertiliser-based explosives to preparing larger quantities of IEDs. The module is accused of being behind the suicide bombing near the Red Fort on Nov 10 last year that killed 15 people and injured 29 others.The explosives trail began close to Al-Falah University. In September-October last year, Umer, Ganaie and Jasir Bilal Wani, a student accused of assisting the module, allegedly tested nitro-glycerine near a tubewell on the campus. The explosive had reportedly been prepared at Ganaie’s flat.The group then moved its experiments outside the university, carrying out test blasts in an isolated field before venturing deeper into the Faridabad Aravalis. In a forested area of Dhauj, Umer and Ganaie allegedly conducted further tests using TATP (triacetone triperoxide). NIA said remnants of a pipe-like device used in one such test were later recovered at Ganaie’s instance.The chargesheet said the module initially worked with fertiliser-based mixtures before shifting to TATP after tests demonstrated its destructive potential. The experiments eventually progressed to the preparation of larger quantities of IEDs.The weapons trail ran parallel to the explosives experiments. NIA alleged that Dr Shaheen Shahid, an associate professor in Al-Falah’s pharmacology department, provided around Rs 16 lakh to members of Ansar Ghazwat-ul-Hind (AGuH), a militant outfit founded in Kashmir in 2016 and linked to al-Qaida’s ideology. The agency alleged that the money, routed through Ganaie, was used to procure a Krinkov rifle, an AK-47 and two pistols.During Adeel’s visit to Al-Falah in October-November 2024, Ganaie, Adeel and Shaheen allegedly test-fired the Krinkov in another forested area of Dhauj. NIA further alleged that rented premises in Khori Jamalpur and Dhauj were later used to store chemicals, equipment and explosives away from public view.The procurement of material was also allegedly systematic. Umer, Ganaie, Shaheen and Wani visited markets in Gurgaon and Faridabad to buy fertilisers, chemicals, electrical equipment, trolley bags, collapsible water bags, gas stoves and other material needed for the preparations. The items were initially kept in flats on the Al-Falah campus before being shifted to rented premises near Dhauj.Wani, a Qazigund resident and political science graduate, allegedly provided technical assistance to the group. NIA said he repeatedly visited Al-Falah, helped prepare explosives and assisted in shifting raw materials to rented premises. He also allegedly prepared rocket-type IEDs while staying in Umer’s room.By early 2025, the module had allegedly fabricated several “suitcase-type IEDs” and shifted part of the stock to another rented property in Dhauj. A major cache was subsequently recovered from Fatehpur Taga, where around 2,600kg of ammonium nitrate was seized on Nov 9, a day before the Red Fort blast.Umer, identified by NIA as the suicide bomber, was killed when the i20 he was driving exploded near the crowded metro station. The blast killed 15 people and injured 29 others.The chargesheet also shed light on why Umer allegedly continued working at Al-Falah despite receiving a higher-paying job offer in Pathankot. According to NIA, the university gave him access to chemicals, fertilisers, electrical equipment, vehicles, firearms and members of AGuH.“That is because if Umer had chosen to move out of Al-Falah, his entire racket for hatching conspiracy with the co-accused and others would not have taken shape,” the chargesheet stated.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Gurgaon | Silver Rate in Gurgaon | Bank Holidays in Gurgaon | Public Holidays in Gurgaon | Gurgaon AQI | Weather in Gurgaon | Petrol Price in Gurgaon | Diesel Price in Gurgaon | CNG Price in Gurgaon | LPG Price in GurgaonStay updated with the latest Gurgaon news.
