articles.title: Taiwan vice president makes rare Europe visit for conference on democracy
articles.summary: European Parliament’s Pina Picierno says Hsiao’s visit ‘was kept secret until her arrival to protect her participation’.
articles.body:
Taiwanese Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim is making a rare visit to Europe, attending a forum on democracy in Italy alongside the island’s foreign minister, the presidential office said.

Hsiao has been invited to attend the Ventotene Conference for Freedom and Democracy, and is travelling with Taiwanese Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung, the presidential office said in a brief statement.

Other details will be provided once the two return to Taiwan from the Italian island of Ventotene, it added

While Taiwan’s foreign ministers occasionally visit Europe and other parts of the world that have no formal ties to the Chinese-claimed island, it is rare for an official as senior as the vice president to do so, given the risk of backlash from Beijing against the host nation.

Pina Picierno, vice president of the European Parliament, said Hsiao’s planned participation “was kept secret until her arrival to protect her participation” in the conference.

“No one can determine who can be hosted on European soil, what voices can be heard, and what presences must be hidden,” Picierno said in a Facebook post. “It is a simple and very clear message: intimidation cannot decide who participates in our democratic debate.”

“Freedom of debate is not negotiable with autocracies. And Ventotene, more than ever today, must continue to be the place where freedom and democracy are defended without fear,” she added.

The Ventotene conference takes place from Thursday until Saturday this week. Italy, like most countries, has no formal diplomatic ties with Chinese-claimed Taiwan.

Oleksandra Matviichuk, a 2022 Nobel Peace Prize laureate and president of Ukraine’s Centre for Civil Liberties, is also expected to participate in the conference.

China says Taiwan is one of its provinces, a view the democratically governed island strongly rejects.

Last November, Hsiao spoke at the Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China’s annual summit, held in the European Parliament in Brussels.

articles.title: Entrepreneur-actor Parul Gulati shares her 3-post social media strategy, says, ‘People want different things at different times’
articles.summary: Work & Career News: Instagram can often feel like a guessing game for creators and businesses. Post too much, and audiences may tune out. Post too little, and the algorit.
articles.body: Instagram can often feel like a guessing game for creators and businesses. Post too much, and audiences may tune out. Post too little, and the algorithm may stop favouring your content. But according to entrepreneur and actor Parul Gulati, the answer may lie not just in what you post, but in when you post it.Speaking on the podcast Restless With Ayush Shukla, Gulati explained the three-post-a-day strategy she follows for her business, Nish Hair. The approach is built around a simple observation: people's mindset changes as the day progresses, and social media content can be planned around those changing moods.Morning is for sales“Morning posts are designed to drive direct sales when people are starting their day,” says Gulati.According to her, the logic is straightforward. In the morning, when people are starting their day and potentially planning what they need to buy, the content focuses more directly on the product and its purpose. Rather than treating every Instagram post as an opportunity to entertain, this strategy gives the first post a clear commercial role.For businesses trying to turn social media attention into actual revenue, this is an important distinction. Not every post needs to go viral. Some posts simply need to help a potential customer understand what is being offered and encourage them to make a purchase.Afternoon is about grabbing attentionThe second post has a different job. “Afternoon posts grab attention with high-quality visual launches,” notes Gulati. According to her, at this point, the aim is less about directly pushing a sale and more about making people stop scrolling.High-quality pictures, visually appealing launches and content that immediately catches the eye become important here. It reflects a broader lesson for anyone building a brand online: social media users are constantly being exposed to new information. A product may be useful, but usefulness alone does not guarantee attention. Presentation matters too.The afternoon post, therefore, works almost like a visual showcase- something designed to make people pause, look and remember.Evening is when the strategy gets playfulThe third post is perhaps the most interesting part of Gulati's approach. “Evening posts are purely lighthearted and funny to capture people scrolling after work.” She said the evening content is more "gimmicky" and humorous, because people are scrolling after work and are looking for something they can simply enjoy.Her reasoning is rooted in audience behaviour. By the evening, people have largely moved away from the workday mindset. Instead of another straightforward product message, they may be more receptive to something funny, relatable or entertaining.Gulati explained that such content could make people laugh while also connecting with a familiar problem- such as hair fall. If the post is visually appealing, funny and relatable at the same time, viewers are more likely to remember it."People are laughing at night," she said while explaining the thinking behind the evening strategy.The bigger lesson for creators and businessesWhat makes the strategy interesting is that the three posts are not simply three versions of the same advertisement. Each one has a different purpose: morning content is meant to sell, afternoon content is meant to attract attention, and evening content is meant to entertain.For professionals, creators and small businesses trying to build an audience, this offers a useful way of thinking about content calendars. Instead of asking only, "What should I post today?", the better question could be, "What is my audience likely to want from me at this time of the day?"The approach also shows why building an online brand is increasingly about understanding audience behaviour rather than simply producing more content. A successful social media strategy does not necessarily mean posting constantly. It means giving each piece of content a reason to exist. Gulati's three-post formula essentially divides the day into three different opportunities: conversion, attention and connection.And for anyone trying to turn Instagram from a social platform into a serious business tool, that distinction could be more valuable than chasing the next viral trend.Get the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. articles.title: Republican midterm convention wraps up in Dallas, Texas: Key takeaways
articles.summary: Protesters gather on final night as US Republicans seek to rally base ahead of consequential legislative elections.
articles.body:
Dallas, Texas – Night two of the first-of-its-kind Republican midterm convention has wrapped up, with the party officially hitching its wagon to US President Donald Trump as it faces uphill legislative elections in November.

On the first night , speaker after speaker portrayed an existential fight against an increasingly “radical” Democratic Party. In his keynote address, Trump urged voters on Wednesday to “pretend” he is on the ballot, even as entrenched concerns over affordability, fuelled by the US-Israel war on Iran, have seen the president’s approval ratings dive.

Going a step further, Trump also pledged to give US citizens a “$5,000 dividend” if Republicans hold onto both the House of Representatives and the Senate in the elections, a promise that met with consternation from both his supporters and critics.

Night two saw more efforts to rally the Republican base. Here were the key takeaways.

The Democratic National Committee opted not to hold its own national convention, an event typically held only during presidential election cycles.

Instead, the liberal response was largely contained to a small protest held near the American Airlines Center, where the Republican convention was taking place, with Democrats holding a rally at Dallas City Hall in the evening.

“It’s to bring national attention to this and hopefully put some pressure on politicians that aren’t so firmly rooted in MAGA,” said Jon Pattison, 66, from Frisco, Texas, a retiree and activist with the Indivisible group, which organised the protest near the American Airlines Center.

The convention “is going to have the opposite effect from what Trump wants. Like rats from a sinking ship”, he said.

“We’re gonna flip Texas, and Trump is worried about it,” he added.

Kathryn Suarez, 51, a project manager from Dallas, said Republicans were “threatened by James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa”, referring to the Democratic Senate candidate Talarico, who has been pulling away from Republican candidate Ken Paxton, and Democratic gubernatorial candidate Hinojosa.

“It’s no secret that Texas is generally a red state, so [the convention] may work in [Trump’s] favour,” she said. “But that’s why we’re here; to try to stand up and make sure that people know that that’s not the only option.”

But despite Trump’s overall low approval rating, Texas-based Democratic strategist Rania Batrice warned that the Democratic leadership has still failed to articulate a clear message to meet the moment in the final stretch of the election.

“There are individuals running for office who are capturing that moment, who are showing up in that moment,” she told Al Jazeera. “I think James Talarico is one of them. Abdul El-Sayed is obviously one of them.”

“They’re doing what our leadership is not doing,” Batrice said.

Vice President JD Vance delivered Thursday’s keynote speech after being bumped from Wednesday night by Trump.

Focusing largely on traditional “family values” issues and praising Trump’s immigration policies, Vance appealed for Republican unity, even amid disagreements.

He pointed to slain conservative activist Charlie Kirk’s opposition to foreign wars. Vance has been widely seen as one of the most critical voices of the US-Israel war on Iran in the Trump administration.

“I’m not asking anybody to agree with me on every single issue,” he said. “I’m not asking anybody to agree on every single policy of the administration.”

“What I am asking you to do is to recognise the contrast with the radicals and recognise the achievements of the last 18 months. We have done a lot, my friends, and we can do a lot more if we fight together,” he said.

Vance has long led polls of potential Trump successors, and the high-profile speech is likely to further solidify his role as the heir apparent.

While many who spoke to Al Jazeera saw Vance as Trump’s most likely successor in 2028, several also saw Secretary of State Marco Rubio as the man for the job.

“I like Rubio,” said Brendan House, a 42-year-old resident of Shreveport, Louisiana.

“He’s a jack of all trades,” he said, referring to Rubio’s multiple roles beyond top diplomat, including head of the largely defunct USAID agency and acting archivist at the National Archives.

“I feel like Trump has been grooming him for the job,” he said.

Some voters were eyeing champions from farther afield.

Ronnda Law, a 55-year-old from Lubbock, Texas, hoped conservative podcaster Tucker Carlson would step into the race.

“He’s a Christian. He’s anti-sending all of our money and our men to die for Israel, which is something that’s happened forever,” she said.

Texas lawmakers say banning ‘Sharia law’ a Republican priority

Two Texas officials used their speeches on Thursday to decry “ Sharia law “, highlighting the issue as a Republican priority.

“Sharia law has no place in America,” Senator Ted Cruz said. “Sharia law is fundamentally inconsistent with the Constitution, and we need to stand together and stop it now.”

His statement comes as Republicans in Congress have increasingly seized on the concept, launching a so-called “Sharia-free America caucus”.

Critics have said lawmakers have misrepresented the Islamic concept of Sharia, which roughly translates to “the trodden path to water”. Lawmakers have made no meaningful effort to codify interpretations of Islamic principles into US law. Advocates have accused lawmakers of fabricating an issue to stigmatise Islam .

In Texas, the Republican-controlled government has taken several actions decried by advocates as Islamophobic, including a recent effort to ban prayer ablution areas at airports.

Governor Greg Abbott, who also spoke on Thursday, has also sought to label the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR) in Texas as a foreign “terrorist” organisation.

“We are not waiting on Washington, DC,” he said during his speech. “We will fully ban Sharia law in Texas.”

Michigan’s El-Sayed gets brunt of attacks

While Texas Democratic Senate candidate Talarico received outsized attention on Wednesday, Thursday saw a heavier focus on Michigan progressive Abdul El-Sayed .

Republican candidate Mike Rogers criticised El-Sayed over campaign appearances he made with left-wing streaming commentator Hasan Piker.

“Abdul El-Sayed has chosen Hasan as his running mate,” Rogers said. “Together, they attack America. They excuse extremism. They treat our country like it’s the villain.”

So far, El-Sayed has refused to repudiate comments from Piker, who has accused critics of intentionally taking statements out of context.

On Wednesday, Republican Congressman Tom Emmer, in a falsehood-laden diatribe, suggested that the US-born El Sayed should leave the country.

“If you don’t love America, get the hell out,” Emmer said.

El-Sayed, for his part, released a new attack advertisement against Rogers on Thursday.

Trump further solidifies outsized role in midterms

If one message was clear during the two-day convention, it was that Trump will remain a defining force in the final stretch of the midterm election.

On Wednesday, he pledged to rally for every tight Senate and House race in the coming weeks, a potentially disconcerting notion for candidates wary of associating with the increasingly unpopular president.

On Thursday, Trump reiterated that Republicans needed to vote in the midterm elections as if he were on the ballot. He again promised every American adult a $5,000 payment if Republicans keep control of Congress, without providing details.

He acknowledged relying on the military “a little more than I thought”, but insisted that Iran would never obtain a nuclear weapon, and again referred to the Strait of Hormuz as the “Trump strait”.

Speaking to Al Jazeera, congressional candidate Gerald Molloy, who is running to unseat progressive Becca Balint in deep-blue Vermont, said he understood why some candidates in liberal-leaning states might be wary of Trump’s embrace.

“I tell Vermonters, it’s not about the White House. It’s about delivering results from DC,” he said.

Still, he said he believed that the wider framing of the race, one of “common sense” Republicans against increasingly “radical” Democrats, would prove potent with voters.

“What I do think was kind of the theme of the whole [convention] was, you’ve got the GOP and here’s your other choice: socialism, DSA,” he said, referring to the Democratic Socialists of America, who are set to grow their presence in Congress this election cycle.

“I think we kind of drove home why the GOP is the right choice, and the choice right now,” he said.

articles.title: ‘I’m coming home’: Last words haunt a 9/11 daughter 25 years later as she builds a legacy in his honor
articles.summary: Kayla Fallon Smith lost her father in the 9/11 World Trade Center attacks at age 8 and now runs a nonprofit offering equine therapy to veterans.
articles.body: "I'm getting out. I'm coming home." Those were the final words of William Lawrence Fallon Jr. before he was killed in the 9/11 terrorist attacks on the World Trade Center 25 years ago. He worked as an IT manager for Cantor Fitzgerald and was just 38 years old when he was killed. I LOST MY WIFE ON 9/11. PLEASE LET THIS 25TH ANNIVERSARY BELONG TO THE FAMILIES His daughter Kayla Fallon Smith was 8 years old when she learned her father would not be coming home. Before the attacks, Smith, now 33, said her father – who always commuted into work early – would call the house phone in the morning to wish her and her sister well before they would head to school. 📩 Send me a story idea: kelsie.cairns@fox.com 📸 Instagram: kelsiecairns_tv 🎥 Facebook: Kelsie Cairns He went in early so he could leave earlier in the afternoons to take her to dancing school after her school day. "That was the kind of man he was. I remember he would get up and work out in the morning before even going to work, so you'd hear the weights dropping in the house. I do remember that as a kid," Smith said. Those quick and light-hearted morning phone calls to his daughters set the tone for the day. "He would tell us what the skyline looked like. Sometimes it would be cloudy below him and he couldn't even see the street, but it'd be sunny up there," she said. FRANK SILLER: 'I LOVE YOU, BROTHER' -- THE 9/11 LOSS THAT INSPIRED A MISSION OF SERVICE Smith remembers hearing her father's voice for the last time on Tuesday, Sept. 11, 2001. "I spoke to him on the house phone that day, as I always did," she said, to which he said on the phone, "Have a good morning," she said. "I'm sure I said something like, 'I love you, have a great day'," Smith said. Her dad called again that fateful morning – sometime after the first tower was hit. SALVATION ARMY RESPONDER OPENS UP ON 9/11 CANCER BATTLE, PHONE CALL THAT CHANGED HIS LIFE This time, her mother answered the phone. "He said something to the degree of, 'I'm getting out, I'm coming home,' and that was it," she said. Smith's mother replied and said, "What are you talking about?" He responded and said, "Turn on the news." After that he hung up. 9/11 DEATH TOLL KEEPS GROWING DECADES LATER AS TOXIC EXPOSURE HAUNTS SURVIVORS His family never heard from him again. "Those words haunt me a little bit," Smith said. "Every year, grief is different. It doesn't go away. It's a myth when people say that time heals all wounds; it doesn't." In the last 25 years of growing up without her father, Smith has turned her pain and grief into purpose. She's devoted her life to helping others living with grief and mental struggles. FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X Smith is a licensed mental health counselor who founded Trails of Purpose – a nonprofit organization that provides free mental health counseling and equine-assisted therapy to military members, veterans, first responders and their families. "As I was getting my graduate degree, I started to experience equine-assisted therapy, and I really—it just clicked for me," she said. She went on to say, "I never experienced that as a kid, and I had a lot of trauma therapy growing up. The resources were abundant for 9/11 victims, and I never experienced equine therapy." I think I've created that, and it's seeming to resonate with other people." SEND US A TIP Trails of Purpose has offered 30,000 hours of free mental health counseling and equine-assisted therapy to military members and first responders. GOT A TIP? "The horses, and the connection that they have when when words don't seem to to come, the horses can just be with you," she said. articles.title: Japan’s feminist performers use ‘cute’ fashion to confront rape, harassment and sexism
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In a Tokyo theatre, women in elaborate dresses and wide, bell-shaped skirts scream about rape, harassment and the pressures placed on women in Japan.T.
articles.body: In a Tokyo theatre, women in elaborate dresses and wide, bell-shaped skirts scream about rape, harassment and the pressures placed on women in Japan.The performers belong to TremendousCircus, a self-described radical feminist theatre group that uses Gothic Lolita fashion and stories of sexual violence to challenge a society they say remains dominated by men.During a recent three-hour performance called “Unite”, nine women dressed in pink, white and black portrayed revolutionaries fighting an artificial intelligence ruler called “Big Father”. They shouted slogans including “war for women” and tore apart AI-generated images of men.The group’s work comes as Japan continues to struggle with sexual violence and gender inequality. The global #MeToo movement has had limited impact in the country, while many survivors remain afraid to speak publicly.Turning fashion into resistanceTremendousCircus began in 2016 with a focus on LGBTQ rights. Its members now describe their approach as “radical victim feminism”, which places the experiences and needs of sexual violence survivors at the centre of its work.The troupe’s performers wear Gothic Lolita clothing, a style inspired by Victorian dresses and Gothic imagery. The outfits usually include blouses, jumper skirts, petticoats and layers of fabric that create a voluminous silhouette.Chino, a 28-year-old actor and rape survivor who helped found the group, said the clothing challenged expectations about how women should dress."My goal is to be a role model who can show that a joyful future can await sexual violence survivors," she told news agency AFP.Chino recently concluded a legal battle linked to her own case. She said she did not want the assault to determine the rest of her life."I want to wear pretty clothes and go explore a lot of places," she said."That single moment when I was raped is far shorter than a whole life ahead of me that I should care about and try to enrich."The troupe charges male spectators up to twice as much as women, highlighting Japan’s persistent gender pay gap. Japan ranked 118th out of 148 economies in the World Economic Forum’s Global Gender Gap Index last year.Chino said the group’s clothing was the opposite of the revealing outfits that some men prefer."We can repel men while wearing pretty clothes," she said.Member Hina Haruka, 27, also wears Gothic Lolita clothing away from the stage. In the summer heat, she uses a white lace parasol and bonnet along with her layered dress. "These cannot be easily taken off, so they help protect women from rape as well," she said.She believes the style allows women to express themselves without giving up their femininity."In the Gothic Lolita world we can wear pink and go all out with frills and cuteness no matter how old we are," she said."That makes me think I'm fulfilling the version of myself that I love, and valuing my feelings as a woman -- there's something very feminist about that."A message aimed at all womenChino said radical victim feminism could bring women together because every woman is affected in some way by a society shaped by misogyny.The group does not reject relationships, marriage, motherhood or sex with men. Instead, it says women should be able to choose how they live, including women who are mothers or sex workers.Former sex worker Mizuki Shikyoin said she had been systematically “groomed” by a male boss. During “Unite”, she delivered a monologue about how she had misunderstood what men had given her."Now I know. Everything I thought was 'given' by a boyfriend or a pimp through rape and sex was in fact what was taken away from me," the 27-year-old said.She told AFP that she had once believed she could not manage without men."I used to think I was helpless without men, but I was wrong. I can't do everything alone, but when women help each other we can do anything," Shikyoin said.The message moved many in the audience, most of whom were women. Some smiled while others cried as the performance ended.Ayaka, a 37-year-old audience member who gave only her first name, said the show had helped her understand how deeply society is centred on men."It made me realise how our society is centred around men and understand why my life hasn't gone well sometimes," she said."I can live a bit more positively now."Japan’s government said in a 2024 survey that around one in 10 young people had experienced groping at least once, with women making up the overwhelming majority of victims. TremendousCircus says its performances are an attempt to turn those experiences into a collective demand for change.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: A 14-year-old Welsh teen taught himself football freestyle on YouTube; he now holds five Guinness World Records and has finished third in the world
articles.summary: UK News: A self-taught teenage football freestyler from South Wales who learned ball control by watching online tutorials has won a bronze medal at the World F.
articles.body: A self-taught teenage football freestyler from South Wales who learned ball control by watching online tutorials has won a bronze medal at the World Freestyle Football Association (WFFA) World Championship. James Taylor, a 14-year-old schoolboy from Penarth, Vale of Glamorgan, finished third in his age category at the global event, adding another major achievement to his growing career. According to reports by the BBC and Yahoo News, Taylor faced some of the best young freestyle footballers from around the world after reaching the final rounds through a series of technical knockout battles. Along with his world championship medal, Taylor has also set five Guinness World Records for technical football tricks, all before finishing his secondary education at Stanwell School.Self-taught skills and rapid record successTaylor started practising freestyle football in his back garden while still at primary school. He used online platforms such as YouTube to study difficult tricks, acrobatic moves and ball-juggling routines, often watching the videos frame by frame. "I started by watching videos online and just practicing in my garden every single day," Taylor said in an interview featured in the BBC documentary My Life: Fearless Freestyle. "I saw people doing tricks and thought I really want to learn how to do that." His hard work soon led to world record attempts. According to the Penarth Times, Taylor set his first Guinness World Record when he was 11 during a half-time performance at Cardiff City Stadium. He later broke four more records, with his fifth coming in the under-16 category for completing the most "around the world" tricks in one minute. Guinness World Records adjudicator Glenn Pollard officially verified the fifth record at Cardiff City Stadium. "I'm really happy to have broken my fifth world record and it was great to return to Cardiff City Stadium to do this," Taylor told the Penarth Times. "The 'around the world' move is one of my favourite moves so it was great to get a world record for this football trick."A family tradition on the global stageTaylor's success has also turned freestyle football into a family activity. His 11-year-old younger brother, Ben Taylor, has taken up the sport and has already secured three Guinness World Records in youth freestyle categories. Together, the brothers hold eight verified Guinness World Records. After setting his fifth world record, Taylor went on to win podium places at youth competitions across Europe, including open events in Italy and the Netherlands. His performances eventually helped him earn a place at the WFFA World Championship. Despite his quick rise and international competitions, Taylor continues to balance regular training with his school studies in Wales. His journey was featured in the BBC documentary My Life: Fearless Freestyle, made for CBBC and BBC iPlayer. The programme followed his training around local locations including Penarth Pier and Cosmeston Lakes. Taylor continues to prepare for upcoming European and international competitions while working towards more official world records in freestyle football.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
